title: How many automated tests are too many for an indie game?
author: dnr424
selftext:
I'm still in the early graybox stage. Somehow, the test suite has already grown to over 3,300 tests.

Each feature iteration now takes around 20–30 minutes, including implementation and testing.

Is this normal for AI-assisted game development, or am I overengineering things? How do you guys keep development iterations fast without compromising stability?

comments.author: StellarSoupStudio
comments.body: I'm at 1,723 tests for my game? Development has been good, are you using rust as well?

replies.author: dnr424
replies.body: I'm using GDscript.

replies.author: ail-san
replies.body: Ask Claude to do everything in rust. It’s much faster if your game is demanding

replies.author: DuskLab
replies.body:
And when you find the rust builds even slow, add nextest, build sequencing so GPU-intensive tests don't crush each other in parallel, and crate caching of the target directories. I'm running a pure rust test cycle on 1.5M lines across about 80 crates on the local machine in literally under 3 seconds with over 90% test coverage.

The complaints about rust compile times is a skill issue when AI can build your compilation tooling.

replies.body: For a plugin I am building I also use visual tests. I let it start the programm with the plugin, and let it screenshot everything. Works well to fix optical problems or real user interactions, which he doesn’t noticed because headless tests work fine.

replies.author: Sasbe93
replies.body:
Automated tests are very important. Especially for vibecoded software. Otherwise you have to test each already implemented feature and performance run by yourself each time you implemented new code.

As example:

\-You add a shot feature  
\-You add a jump feature  
\-you test it by yourself-it works, also together  
\-you add and test a charging gun feature, test it with the jump feature together, it worked-you never did it again  
\-you add an enemy, that can deny your charging, you test it while not jumping- it worked  
\-After 3 days you notice the games crashs if the enemy denies your charging, while your are jumping- it cost your agent a lot more tokens and time to fix it, because there is much more code to read. Also it could happen that its editing will not work and you have to test this scenario each time by yourself.  
\-Then you fix it, but 3 days later the problem is back, because your ai blocked important code to add another feature or make it performanter and you don’t even noticed, because the situations are too specific.

So just add tests everywhere you can and run it in intervals, so this shit can‘t happen in the first place.

PS: Also add an automated replay feature with logs about everything. So if you noticed a bug and don‘t know how to reproduce it, just send your agent the log file of your last run and it will find it out for you.

comments.author: scotchable
comments.body: It's normal, but it is annoying. I will often put in guardrails that my agent teams are only to verify the task and run that areas unit tests. Full suite runs are overnight only or by my specific request. Otherwise I'll lose most of my day to tests when I could have been play testing.

comments.author: throndir
comments.body:
For general software development as a whole, you typically want double the lines of test code as source code. AI just making test suite development a lot easier these days, super easy for people to skip out on these for personal or small projects.

You'll want to start iterating on multiple features per session running in parallel.

comments.author: angrydeanerino
comments.body: LLMs in general tend to create a shit ton of unit tests. There are people just completely deleting their whole testing suite.

comments.author: Fate_Drawn
comments.body:
Same thing happened to me. My tests kept growing and every change started taking longer and longer. 

What helped was splitting it up:  
**While working:** a quick test run of about 2 minutes, plus only the tests for the part I'm changing.  
**At night:** the heavy stuff runs automatically. Mostly balance tests: thousands of simulated battles to check that no card, faction or rarity is too strong or too weak. On top of that, the full test suite runs on my main branch. In the morning I get a summary, and if something broke or a card is suddenly way off, that's the first thing I fix.

So I keep the stability, but I don't wait half an hour after every small tweak. A test only has to run when it can tell you something about what you just changed.

comments.author: FondantIcy866
comments.body: Noob here. Can you explain what you mean "test suite", like there are 3300 different tests that are run...each time you change a feature/code? Thanks.

replies.author: dnr424
replies.body: It's to test if game is working as intended. Yes, they're run for every new change but I've made some optimizations to run a small set of tests based on the change being done.

replies.author: FondantIcy866
replies.body: Thanks that makes sense. Can you explain what the optimizations are? Because I’ve had the same problem where it spends half an hour testing after I just made a minor change that has nothing to do with most of the code or game.

replies.author: dnr424
replies.body:
Here are few this I've done
- run tests in parallel 
- only testing what file changed : test script looks at which files are edited and runs only tests related to them.
- splitting up big files & refactor.

Just ask LLM Opus5.5 or GPT sol6.1 to optimise it. It'll plan better.

replies.author: FondantIcy866
replies.body: Thanks! I'm asking you because the LLM is sometimes going astray or making bloated things or running an entire battery of tests every time it changes one tiny thing.

replies.author: natsuzoze
replies.body: That might be the problem, to run everything, every time. I mean, sure it’s great, everything is always tested but at what price? You could find a middle ground and run it once a day as a non regression test sequence. Run all the tests of the feature you work on all the time but the whole test suite only at set interval to make sure there is no unintended regression. Just an idea

replies.body: I'll consider this.

comments.author: Careless_Road8873
comments.body:
3,300 isn't the problem by itself, the run time is. What helped me: tests per mechanic, not per change (does the damage formula hold, does a save load, does the AI pick a legal move), plus a test for every bug that actually happened so it can't come back. While iterating I only run the tests for what I touched, and the full suite runs in the background before I call something done. Mine is about 400 test files / 8k checks and the full run is \~6 min on 3 cores, which I can live with.

Red flags I'd look for: tests that check how the code is written instead of what the game does (they break on every refactor and tell you nothing), and AI writing 20 near-identical tests for one feature. Ask it to merge them into one test with a table of cases.

In graybox I'd keep tests on the things that are expensive to break later: saves, the core rules, anything with numbers. UI and feel you test by playing.

comments.author: StoneCypher
comments.body:
tell your ai to separate your tests into full tests and dev tests, and to aim for a 9:1 ratio.  tell it that the goal is to have the dev tests catch the things that would generally come up, and to be much faster for your iteration loop.  the extensive tests should be kept, but only run on commit, not every single loop.

after that, tell it to split your dev tests into test sets that can run in parallel.

comments.author: geddy
comments.body:
This may not apply, but if the game is web-based, see what you can move into unit tests instead since those run lightning fast.

Otherwise yeah, it's pretty normal and also annoying. Every time I go to deploy and it gives me the final check, "do you want to run the full suite of e2e tests?" I pause and begrudgingly say.. "*ok".*

comments.author: BSwayzeYo
comments.body: My project has a 17,000+ suite it runs after every commit - I make sure it doesn’t do the time consuming testing until I approve the run and I usually don’t do that until between 5 and 10 commits have been made.

comments.author: InternetMagic_n_Tech
comments.body:
As a web-dev of like 20+ years exp... sometimes unit tests cover the same unit 2-3 times for stupid small stuff.  So going off a number isn't useful because it's really about the complexity of your code.

If anything you should check for coverage reports for uncovered lines

But at some point you should refactor your unit tests

Plus godot isn't really great of unit test because you need to set stuff up.

So if you want to reduce your test run time you might need to build some test scenes/stands

comments.author: uayme
comments.body:
I was in this situation a month ago. Claude likes to write tests for every change it makes. And they often broke after simple changes, which took tokens and time to fix. 

Tell your agents file to only write sanity tests for basic scenarios, and to bundle several checks within one 'unit' test if possible. You won't need anything more at a sandbox stage, unless you're doing something crucial for the game to function.

Also, instruct agents to not run whole tests suite after each change, only after a whole implemented feature.

comments.author: Heath_co
comments.body:
I recently upgraded my CPU to compile my engine and blast through those tests. Just yesterday my agents were running a one time ray tracing test that took 4 hours. It would have taken 8 on my old CPU

But I am going to do a test culling round in the next few updates.

comments.author: lelandrangel
comments.body: That’s a lot of tests, man! They say you can never have enough?

comments.author: fapfap_ahh
comments.body:
Setup lanes for your tests. Full, fast, skip, etc. 

Big enough changes can warrant the full lane.

Minor changes fast laned by running the tests that are relevant to the changes.

Comments / etc go in the skip lane.

Remember to also review the tests you have, often. 
Some can be grouped together so you don't rebuild / reload the same things over and over. Some can be deleted due to overlap. Pin down slow tests that are allocating unnecessary assets. Things like that.

comments.author: PlaidWorld
comments.body: Ask the AI to only run the tests is needs to when working on a thing. Then at the end it can run the full test set for starters. Also you can ask the AI to audit your test and make sure you need them all. Also you can have the AI profile all your tests and see what is actually using up all the time. BTW  3,300  seems like way way to many tests for most AI projects I see on discord.

replies.body:

comments.author: TheHarrowed
comments.body: The amount of tests is really situational but I just want to recommend that you perform your testing adversarially. If you allow the same session thats writing your code to also basically test it's own work, time and time again we see that models will cut corners and fill the test suite with fluff and redundancy, as keeping you happy is often a more important goal than rigorous verification of the codebase. Always use a separate session/instance/model to run the tests and you will find that the outcome is always much more worthwhile, and beneficial to your project overall.
